1:
Henry will not have the phrase taken for a mere ending. Death is a way, he says, not only a period of this life but a passage to a better; it is the way of all the earth because all who dwell there are themselves earth and must return to it, so even the heirs of heaven must go it, though they walk it with pleasure, and prophets and kings go it to a brighter honour than prophecy or sovereignty. Gill takes the words plainly as the path none are exempted from, kings or peasants, and adds a dating inference, that David seems to have borrowed the phrase from Joshua, which shows that book was written in his day. Clarke answers from the Latin poets, quoting one of them three times on the pale death that knocks at palace and cottage with one foot, and Blair on the tomb as the appointed rendezvous where all travellers meet.

What be strong and show thyself a man requires is disputed four ways. Keil and Delitzsch reject outright the reading that it means bear my departure bravely, holding that the courage is to show itself in obedience, since the object is appended by the copula and the phrase to keep the keeping of Jehovah always takes its sense from the context. Clarke turns it into a charge to act like a rational being and not a brute, adding that whoever is most devoted to God acts most like a man. For Henry it is resolution, which those who would keep the charge of the Lord must put on, and he notes the force of such a word to one in years but a child. Ellicott says the same, in spite of his youth.

Henry draws the sharpest distinction in the chapter, between the two promises. That the Messiah should come of David's loins was absolute; that there should not fail him a man on the throne of Israel was conditional, resting on his seed behaving as they should, so that each generation in turn keeps the charge and God continues his word. We never let fall the promise, Henry says, till we let fall the precept; and the authority of a dying father is much, but nothing to that of a living God. Clarke follows the condition to its end: they did not keep it, and the justice of God cut off the entail his mercy had made.

Clarke also takes the five terms of the charge in order, ways, statutes, commandments, judgments and testimonies, and on the judgments states a position larger than the verse: a thing is not good because God has commanded it, nor evil because he has forbidden it, but he has commanded the good because it is in its own nature good and useful, and forbidden the evil because it is in its own nature hurtful.

Ellicott divides the deathbed itself. The general charge he calls noble enough, in harmony with the last words of David on him that ruleth over men being just and ruling in the fear of God, with the everlasting covenant ordered in all things and sure, and with the prayer in Chronicles for Solomon and the people, so that David speaks here in the spirit of a true servant and saint of God. But in the particular charges that follow he sees the worldly prudence of an old statesman, and in one case the trace of a long-remembered grudge, singularly true to imperfect human nature though utterly unworthy of an ideal picture of a hero-king. Gill reports a smaller observation from his Jewish authorities, that the dying man is called only David and not King David, either because Solomon was already anointed and reigning in his stead, or because no man, not even a king, has power in the day of death, having no rule over it while it rules over him.
5:
Whether these charges are justice or vendetta is the chapter's question, and the four answers disagree. Clarke is the most absolute: it would have been an insult to justice not to take Joab's life, David was culpable in delaying so long, by the law of God a man who had murdered Abner and Amasa must die, and had David not laid the duty on Solomon he could not have died in the approbation of his Maker. Henry defends the Shimei charge more narrowly, that it proceeded not from personal revenge but from a prudent zeal for the honour of the government and the covenant God had made with the house, adding that a hoary head, if guilty and forfeited, ought not to be any man's protection from justice. Keil and Delitzsch resolve it by a distinction: David had personally forgiven Shimei, unwilling to mar his restoration with an act of punishment, but the insult offered in his person to the anointed of the Lord, as representative of the rights of God, he could not forgive.

Ellicott grants less and sees more. The charge as to Joab has a certain righteousness, since David could not, and because Joab knew of his great crime dared not, punish him as he deserved; the vividness of the blood of war shed in peace, spirting over girdle and sandals, shows how the horror dwelt on his imagination. Yet Abner's murder, treacherous as it was, had some show of justification in the rough duty of the avenger of blood, and David disclaimed it without calling it inexcusable, while the killing of Amasa was plain revenge for a place taken from Joab, which the broken king dared not blame. That a king with clean hands who owed Joab nothing should punish these was perhaps just and within the letter of the law, though clemency might have spared an old and fallen warrior who had served long and ably. The Shimei charge he calls the most ungenerous of all, a virtual withdrawal of a pardon freely granted, partly dictated by policy since the man was powerful and had made himself champion of the fallen house of Saul, but carrying unmistakable traces of an old grudge rankling still. His sharpest point is an omission: David says nothing of the act he most likely resented, the reckless slaughter of Absalom against his express command, nor deigns to allude to the recent treason.

Clarke then reverses the Shimei sentence by a point of grammar. The negative in hold him not guiltless should, he argues, be understood again in the clause that follows, as Hebrew often repeats a particle without expressing it, so the charge reads bring thou not down his hoary head to the grave with blood; and this, he holds, is how Solomon understood his father. On the practical difficulty Keil and Delitzsch are shrewd: do according to thy wisdom means mark the proper opportunity, since punishing so powerful a man as the commander-in-chief required great wisdom if a rebellion in the army, devoted to him, was not to follow.

Barzillai stands out in pleasant contrast, as Ellicott puts it, and Keil and Delitzsch make the duty of gratitude no less holy to a dying king than the demands of justice, noting that to be among those eating at the table means joining the meals, not merely drawing food from the kitchen. Henry adds that kindnesses received must not be buried in our friends' graves or our own, but returned by our children to theirs. On the burial Gill observes that David slept with his fathers without being buried with them, so the phrase means the state of the dead; Clarke reports the tradition of treasure interred with him and plundered centuries later, gives it little credit, and dismisses the modern show of the tomb, monks and Mohammedans having long united to impose on pilgrims.
12:
What the petition meant decides everything, and the witnesses divide. Henry calls it a treasonable project: Adonijah sought Abishag not out of love but because by her he hoped to renew his claim, or because holding a predecessor's wives was then reckoned a branch of the government, as Absalom thought his pretensions much supported by lying with his father's concubines. It was a small game, Henry says, but he hoped to make it an after-game for the kingdom, and to gain by a wife what he could not gain by force. Ellicott reaches the same suspicion by custom rather than motive: by Eastern usage, to take a king's wives was the known privilege of his successor, which is why Ahithophel gave Absalom that unseemly but politic counsel, so a public espousal of Abishag might have passed for a renewed claim. Solomon sees this at once, he adds, though Bathsheba, strangely enough, does not. Clarke denies the design altogether: it does not appear that Adonijah had any thought of the kingdom in the request, however Solomon understood him, and without further evidence this was a flimsy pretext to imbrue his hands in a brother's blood.

So the execution itself is judged three ways. For Henry it is just and necessary, Adonijah betraying himself into the hands of Solomon's justice while the righteous God left him to himself; many ruin themselves, he warns, because they do not know when they are well done to. Ellicott is divided: he grants the policy but hears in Solomon's answer a bitterness venting itself in irony, which argues some passionate feeling mingled with kingly dignity, not unlike his father's bursts over Nabal, and notes that the king infers the hand of the conspirators, rightly or wrongly, and executes vengeance summarily without granting anyone a trial. Clarke refuses all of it. That this was cruelty needs no proof, since the man was suspected, condemned and slain without a hearing; the fable of the wolf and the lamb applies, and the proverb that it is an easy thing to find a staff to beat a dog with, for we readily find an excuse for whatever we are determined to do. He then turns on a commentator who defended it on the ground that a prince cannot always follow the rules of the most perfect morality, policy and the good of the state often requiring what is contrary to the gospel, calls the maxim diabolical, and remarks that if that is how French kings ruled and ministers judged, the revolution that desolated the land is no wonder.

Two smaller observations run alongside. Ellicott explains the deference Adonijah and Solomon both show Bathsheba from the standing of a queen mother in Eastern monarchies, where the wives of a king, being many, count for little politically while the mother of the reigning king is a person of great dignity, which is why each king's mother is so constantly named; Henry reads the same courtesy as obedience to the fifth commandment, children grown great owing honour to their parents no less than children merely grown up. And Ellicott, comparing Solomon's oath here with David's in the chapter before, finds the difference characteristic: in David we always see the living man whose soul longs after God with a vivid personal devotion, while Solomon is emphatically the king, and in the majesty of his royalty his individual character is almost entirely merged.

Clarke alone raises the question of right behind the whole dispute. The kingdom was Adonijah's by primogeniture, by the voice of the people and by the consent of the high priest; but there was a right paramount to all three, the right of God, whose kingdom it was and whose lieutenants the kings were, and he had a right to give the crown where he pleased, and was pleased to give it to Solomon.
26:
Why Abiathar was spared divides the two critics exactly. Keil and Delitzsch take the handling of him as proof how free Solomon's actions were from personal revenge or excessive severity: the priest had forfeited his life in the conspiracy, yet was merely sent to his fields at Anathoth, told he was indeed a man of death but would not die that day because he had borne the ark, both at its conveyance to Jerusalem and in David's flight from Absalom, which is to say because of his high-priestly dignity. Ellicott denies precisely that: it is not Abiathar's priestly character which protects him but the remembrance of his long friendship to David in adversity, and probably of the promise David made him, perhaps not without remorse, when his own deceit to Ahimelech had drawn Saul's vengeance on the man and his family.

Gill is interested in who had the power. The deposition was by Solomon's authority as king and not as a prophet, he insists against one Roman controversialist who distinguishes so, nor by a college of priests at the king's instance, as another claimed, for which there is no foundation. On the prophecy against Eli's house, Ellicott is careful that the words describe not the purpose but the effect of Solomon's action, the degradation of Ithamar's house in Abiathar and the restoration of Eleazar's in Zadok, to whom as Aaron's elder son the primacy would naturally have belonged; while the tabernacle stood at Gibeon under Zadok and the ark on Zion under Abiathar there may have been something like co-ordination, which the temple must in any case have ended. Clarke says more simply that the priesthood thus reverted to its ancient channel.

On Joab Ellicott makes the chapter's sharpest legal observation. It is strange, he thinks, that Joab stood in no apparent danger when the conspiracy failed; and notable that though the real motive for his death was his renewed support of Adonijah, the sentence mentions nothing but the old murders of David's dying charge. Possibly, he suggests, this was deliberate, to bring the case within that emphatic declaration of the Law that no sanctuary shall protect the wilful and treacherous murderer and that innocent blood left unavenged pollutes the land. He finds it significant too of a monarchy grown stronger in young hands that the old captain once too hard for David should fall without one act of resistance or a word on his behalf, after long faithful service tarnished only once by disloyalty.

Where he fled is not agreed. Keil and Delitzsch are explicit that it was not the tabernacle but the holy tent upon Zion. Gill places it at Gibeon and has Benaiah go up to that great high place; Ellicott allows Gibeon as probable and adds a grim coincidence, that Joab would then fall close to the scene of his own murder of Amasa at the great stone there.

Clarke takes the occasion for the law of sanctuary itself. The altars were so sacred that almost any wretch who reached one found safety, which led to abuse and the perversion of justice, until it became a maxim that the guilty be punished even from the altar, God himself decreeing that the presumptuous murderer be dragged thence. The heathen, he adds, had the same ordinance, and he quotes Euripides to the effect that if an unrighteous man should claim the altar's protection the speaker would drag him to justice without fearing the wrath of the gods, since a wicked man must always suffer. Of the end itself Clarke is plainest: Joab bleeds now for Abner, for Amasa, and for Uriah, two of whom he murdered and of the third's blood he was not innocent; he had done the state much service and they knew it, but he was a murderer, and vengeance would not suffer such to live.
35:
The confinement is read as mercy or as a trap. Henry makes it mercy and test together: Solomon knows how to distinguish crimes and criminals, and though not bound by his father's promise will not go directly against it, so he keeps Shimei from the country seat where he might make mischief among neighbours and holds him at Jerusalem as a prisoner at large, in a city beautiful for situation and the joy of the whole earth, with no reason to complain of such a paradise. It was a fair trial of obedience on easy terms, and even those who perish cannot but own such conditions of pardon unexceptionable, so that their blood rests on their own heads. Clarke agrees about the comfort, that giving him the whole city for a prison could have reduced him to no hardships, and adds the motive, that a seditious man at large in favourable circumstances might do much evil and was better kept under the king's eye.

Ellicott concedes the precaution and then takes it apart. The command was reasonable in itself against treason in a man already powerful and of doubtful fidelity, and the mention of crossing the Kedron shows it aimed at preventing his return to Bahurim. But in the face of David's charge it is difficult to doubt it was in some degree meant as a snare, and Solomon's own words at the end, reaching back to the old offence, confirm it. The narrative gives no hint that the journey to Gath was anything but good faith, simply to recover his slaves; and a command justified by the danger of his living at Bahurim among his own people could hardly be disobeyed in spirit by a temporary journey abroad. Legally the execution was defensible and it may have been politic, Ellicott concludes, but it cannot stand examination on the ground of equity or generosity.

Why he went at all the others try to explain. Gill offers a string of possibilities: passion with his servants, haste, a covetous temper, forgetfulness, a guess that Solomon had forgotten, a hope of going and returning secretly, or a reckoning that no king would exact death for so small a fault; and settles it on providence, God leaving him to his own lust that he might suffer for cursing David. Clarke simply marvels that with his eyes wide open he would run into the jaws of death.

Clarke also returns to his reading of David's charge, and this time argues it from conduct rather than grammar. If the dying king had really ordered Shimei killed, how did Solomon understand him? He did not kill him; having put Joab to death at once in obedience to his father, he sent for Shimei and, knowing the man needed watching, confined him to one city for life. That, Clarke holds with the critic he follows, is the best interpretation of the text, and it clears David of commanding a death he had sworn not to inflict.

The promotions that frame the chapter get a word each. Henry sees in Zadok's elevation the fulfilment of the threat against the house of Eli and the promise of a faithful priest with a sure house, drawing from it that sacred offices may be disgraced but not destroyed by the maladministration of those entrusted with them, nor will God's work stand still for want of hands; and he notes that the ancient right lay with Zadok, of the family of Eleazar, where Eli and his house were of Ithamar. Ellicott observes only that Benaiah succeeds to Joab's command over the host, and that the Hebrew text names no successor at all to his old command over the body-guard. Clarke, closing, thinks Solomon judged that while such men went unpunished the nation could not prosper, and that justice of this kind was required of him for the establishing of his throne.
